title: Postmarked Nine Years Ago
excerpt: The lawyer reads the will. The letter slot opens. Nine years of silence begin arriving.
content:
The will was read on a Tuesday, and the lighthouse turned on that same night — which was impossible, because the power had been cut for a decade.

"Joint inheritance," the lawyer said, not looking up. "Miss Okoye. Mr. Vanterpool. Your grandmother left you the tower, the cottage, and the correspondence."

"What correspondence?" Sade asked.

The lawyer slid a brass key across the desk. "The kind you write."

They drove out together because neither of them trusted the other with the door key, and the whole way the gulls screamed like lawyers with a grudge. Nine summers of rivalry — the regatta, the essay prize, the incident with the pedal boat that both their families still called The Incident — and now a shared lighthouse.

Inside the tower, on the nineteenth step, there was a letter slot that had no business existing. Old, brass, polished. Beside it, a sign in her grandmother's handwriting:

POST HERE. IT WILL BE DELIVERED WHEN IT IS NEEDED.

"She was a romantic," Theo said.

"She was a menace," Sade said.

That night, the light turned on. The power company swore nothing was connected. And on the doorstep of the cottage, at 3:07 in the morning, Sade found an envelope — worn soft at the corners, stamped nine years ago, addressed in her own teenage handwriting.

To Theo Vanterpool, it said.

She read it on the stairs, sitting where the draft couldn't reach, and by the end of the second page her face was the color of the lighthouse beam.

She had written it the summer everything went wrong, and she had never sent it, and now the lighthouse was sending it for her — one truthful, mortifying page at a time.

Upstairs, the slot clacked. Another letter was on its way.
